title: Three Gross Parasites
summary: Josh and Chuck continue their two-part parasite series, tied to Discovery/Animal Planet's Monsters Inside Me. They cover leishmaniasis (cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral forms, transmitted by sand flies, with its life cycle in macrophages), dracunculiasis (guinea worm, spread via contaminated water with water fleas, its emergence from the skin, extraction methods, and eradication efforts by the Carter Center and WHO), and tapeworms (intestinal infection, Taenia species, the pork tapeworm, evolutionary origins, and egg longevity). They also give a shout-out to the human bot fly, which uses mosquitoes to deposit its larvae. The episode closes with listener mail about Superman's promise in the Earthquake episode and a Twinkie shelf-life experiment.

segments.title: Opening banter and parasite series setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about a name generator and introduce the two-part parasite podcast inspired by the Monsters Inside Me website, previewing three gross parasites plus a bonus.

segments.title: Leishmaniasis and sand flies
segments.summary: Leishmaniasis is spread by sand flies, with case counts rising due to climate change and military deployments in the Middle East. The hosts describe the cutaneous form with volcano-shaped sores, the mucocutaneous form that eats away facial tissue, and the dangerous visceral form that affects the liver and spleen. They explain the parasite's life cycle inside macrophages.

segments.title: Guinea worm disease
segments.summary: Dracunculiasis, or guinea worm, comes from drinking contaminated water containing water fleas. The worm grows in the body for months, emerges through a blister when the person enters water, and is removed slowly by winding it around gauze. The hosts note case declines from about 3.5 million to under 10,000 and efforts by the Carter Center and WHO.

segments.title: Transition to tapeworms
segments.summary: Chuck attempts to move on, and Josh and Chuck discuss the timer. They introduce tapeworms as the next parasite.

segments.title: Tapeworms, evolution, and infection
segments.summary: Tapeworms, including Taenia species, may date back about 2.7 million years, and research suggests humans may have passed them to domesticated animals. Infection requires herbivore intermediate hosts for some species, while Taenia solium can infect via undercooked pork or fecal contamination. Eggs can survive about 25 years outdoors, and larvae can lodge in organs, including the brain and eyes.

segments.title: High colonics anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck describes getting high colonics and a story of a customer who passed a ball of worms. The hosts joke about the show's name and warn about sanitation.

segments.title: Human bot fly
segments.summary: Josh offers a shout-out to the human bot fly, which lays eggs on mosquitoes that transfer larvae into mammals. The larvae feed under the skin for several weeks before emerging, and there is no treatment other than popping them out. Robert Lamb's blog post on the topic is mentioned.

segments.title: Show promotion
segments.summary: Hosts promote the Monsters Inside Me show on Animal Planet and the HowStuffWorks blogs.

segments.title: Listener mail: Superman and Twinkies
segments.summary: A listener corrects the claim that Superman lied to Lois Lane in the Earthquake episode, saying he kept his promise. Another listener describes a three-year Twinkie shelf-life experiment at a university newspaper.
